newsitem.title: USA: N.J regulator okays Bell Atlantic settlement.
newsitem.headline: N.J regulator okays Bell Atlantic settlement.

text.p: The New Jersey Board of Public Utilities said Monday it adopted a $176 million settlement among Bell Atlantic Corp, the ratepayer advocate and the board's staff that involves communication integration among the state's schools and libraries

The action will link all of the state's 3,357 public, private and parochial schools and 310 libraries to an advanced electronic network by the end of 2001. The date is nine years sooner than Bell Atlantic's original target, the board said.
Implementation of the program will add 800 technical and service representative jobs to Bell Atlantic's workforce in New Jersey in 1997, the board said.

The system envisioned will allow high speed video, voice and data communications, bringing long-distance, interactive learning to classrooms throughout the state, which will be able to communicate with each other and with the worldwide web of electronic information, it added.
Governor Christie Whitman said the use of the technologies "will open up exciting new avenues of learning for our children that were never before possible."
"The very definition of 'classroom' wil be altered as interactive technology allows students from every part or the state to learn and communicate simultaneously with one another," she said.

The network will be built at a cost of $55 million. Bell Atlantic's New Jersey operation will install up to 22 asynchronous transfer mode (ATM) switches throughout the state. There are currently only two such switches in northern New Jersey and two additonal switches are planned in the southern part of the state.
Bell Atlantic will also set up a $25 million fund to help speed the purchase by schools and libraries of equipment needed to connect to the network.

Bell Atlantic will also make available $50 million in discounts to schools and libraries so they can easily gain access to the network. The state's education department will determine which schools should be equipped and linked to the network.
Through 1999, Bell Atlantic will forego some $28 million in rate adjustments, as part of the settlement.
Businesses in the state's so-called Urban Enterprise Zones will also benefit from the settlement, as it will allow them to be linked to the network within 90 days of making a request.
"This will help businesses in urban areas compete in the global market place, said Herbert Tate, president of the utilities board.

Separately, the board asked Bell Atlantic to expand its plans to provide fiver-to-curb service for households in the northeastern part of the state. The technology will enable residents to hook into the network for electronic services they choose.

The board also said it had favorably reviewed a pending merger between Bell Atlantic and NYNEX Corp. As part of that review it rules that rates for basic local service in the state will remain frozen at 1993 rates until 1999.
The merger is currently under review by the Department of Justice.
